how-much-to-charge-to-pave-a-driveway.ht.text:
← Asphalt driveway paving bid calculator

How much to charge to pave a driveway

A published $3.50-a-square-foot special treats 800 square feet of sound asphalt as the same job as 1,000 square feet with a failed base, a 4-inch street apron, and 60 feet of sawcut at the garage. It is not. Sealcoat calculators price a thin coating and crack fill. Concrete calculators price cubic yards of slab. Paving the driveway is a method, a thickness, and the extra work you have to do before the paver rolls. Quoting all of that from a per-square-foot special is how the first sawcut eats the field margin.

A job with the same square footage can cost much more

Each extra inch of thickness is mix that never appears on the brochure. On the sample rates an 800-square-foot 2-inch overlay with 20 feet of sawcut prices about $3,076 ($3.85 per square foot, 5.6 crew-hours, 9.7 tons, walk-away $2,215). The same shop’s 1,000-square-foot full-depth at 3 inches with 200 square feet of failed base and an 80-square-foot 4-inch apron prices about $6,530 ($6.05 per square foot, 18.2 hours, 20.1 tons). A quarter of that full-depth bid is extra work — demo, dump, gravel, and the apron. Matching the overlay’s $3.85-a-square-foot special on the full-depth driveway is how that job becomes a loss.

Overlay looks cheaper until the base has failed

Overlaying a failed base is a callback, not a savings. On the same 1,000-square-foot driveway the sample rates price a 3-inch overlay at about $5,287 — $1,243 less than full-depth. That gap is demo and gravel, not profit. Mill-and-overlay of that run prices about $5,787. Overlay is still the right bid on sound 800-square-foot work: milling that refresh prices about $3,437 and full-depth about $3,818 because you would be tearing out a driveway that only needed a lift. Treating every driveway as one per-square-foot number is how the method that looked cheapest on paper is not the one that keeps the margin.

A mill-and-overlay with an apron is not automatically the cheap 2-inch job

A 1,200-square-foot mill-and-overlay at 2 inches with an 80-square-foot 4-inch apron is not the 800-square-foot refresh plus 50%. On the sample rates that mill-and-overlay prices about $5,073 ($3.96 per square foot, 11.2 crew-hours, 16.4 tons). Millings are a dump ticket; the apron is extra tons at a thicker lift. A 2,000-square-foot mill-and-overlay at 2.5 inches with fabric over cracks prices about $10,801 ($5.02 per square foot, 33.8 tons). Neither number lives in a $3.50-a-square-foot special.

Load the wage, then keep a walk-away number

A $38/h hand loaded at 32% payroll burden is $50.16. Margin is a share of the price you send, not a markup on cost. The walk-away price is total cost — below that the job makes nothing before you take a dollar home. Replace every rate with your invoices before you send either number.

What this is not

This is arithmetic on the rates you type. It is not a paving specification, a code determination, a permit, an engineering stamp, or a recommendation of overlay versus full-depth. Thickness, base condition, and what the jurisdiction will accept at the street still decide the method. Verify every figure against your own takeoff.

No warranty. This free page is not paving, construction, legal, tax, or financial advice. You are responsible for reviewing and verifying its output before relying on it. It is hosted best-effort with no SLA: it may be slow, broken, moved, or taken offline without notice. Open the bid calculator to price a specific driveway, or see should I only charge material cost for paving fabric?

Common questions

How much to charge to pave a driveway?

Charge from the method (overlay, mill-and-overlay, or full-depth), the square footage, new-asphalt thickness, street apron, failed-base gravel, sawcut, loaded labor, overhead, and a margin that is a share of price. A default 800-square-foot 2-inch overlay at the sample rates in this calculator prices around $3,076 — about $3.85 per square foot.

When is full-depth more than an overlay?

When the existing mat and the base have to come out. On the sample rates a 1,000-square-foot full-depth at 3 inches with 200 square feet of failed base and a 4-inch apron prices around $6,530. Overlaying that same driveway looks cheaper on paper — around $5,287 — until the failed base shows up under the new mat. The per-square-foot special never sees the demo ticket.

How much to charge for mill-and-overlay?

Milling is not an overlay and an overlay is not full-depth. On the sample rates a 1,200-square-foot mill-and-overlay at 2 inches with an 80-square-foot 4-inch apron prices around $5,073 ($3.96 per square foot, 11.2 crew-hours, 16.4 tons). Millings are a dump ticket; the apron is extra tons at a thicker lift.

Bid the method, the thickness, and the extra work.

Price an asphalt driveway the way the trade actually loses money: overlay versus mill-and-overlay versus full-depth, mix tons from thickness, the street apron, failed base, and the sawcut at the garage. 800 square feet of sound asphalt is not the same bid as 1,000 square feet that has to come out.         Common questions

        What does this paving estimate include?

        The price adds up hot-mix tons for the driveway and apron by thickness, milling tons and dump cost for a mill-and-overlay, demo and dump tons for a full-depth replacement, a failed-base gravel patch, sawcut, tack coat, paving fabric when selected, a permit line, travel and equipment, overhead, and your target margin — all from the method, area, and rates you enter, not a flat price list.

        Why does the same driveway price differently as an overlay, mill-and-overlay, or full-depth job?

        Each method starts from its own suggested machine hours and material rates: a full-depth job adds demo and base-gravel hours an overlay never touches, and a mill-and-overlay adds milling hours and dump cost an overlay skips. The three-way comparison prices your same takeoff under each method’s starting kit so you can see when a failed base or a thick apron flips which method is actually cheaper.

        Does it account for the street apron and a failed base separately from the driveway?

        Yes. The apron is its own area and thickness, added to the driveway to get the total paved square footage that drives mix tons and most labor. A failed-base patch is a separate square footage and gravel thickness, capped at the paved area, and its gravel tons and hours only apply where you enter it.

        Is my data uploaded anywhere?

        No account and no network requests — the calculator runs entirely in your browser. Your bid is saved in this browser’s local storage between visits, and a bid link you copy carries those same numbers in the page’s URL hash rather than sending anything to a server.

        What’s the difference between the bid price and the walk-away price?

        The bid price already includes your target margin on top of labor, materials, and overhead. The walk-away price is the total cost underneath it — labor, mix, milling or demo dump, gravel, sawcut, and every other line item — the point below which the job stops being profitable at all.

        Does this check pavement condition, code, or engineering requirements?

        No. Hours and material rates are ballpark shop figures you can edit, not a paving specification, a pavement-condition assessment, or an engineering stamp. Deciding whether a driveway needs a full-depth rebuild rather than an overlay is still a call for the site visit; this tool only prices whichever method you tell it to.

should-i-only-charge-material-cost-for-p.text:
← Asphalt driveway paving bid calculator

Should I only charge material cost for paving fabric?

Paving fabric over cracks has a sticker price: $0.55 a square foot in this calculator's own default rates. On this calculator's fabric-over-cracks preset — a 2,000 sq ft mill-and-overlay plus a 150 sq ft apron, 2,150 sq ft of paved area — that is $1,182.50 of material. It is not what fabric should add to the price you send.

Open the free asphalt driveway paving bid calculator

The material line and the price line are not the same number

Using this calculator's own default crew rates (16% overhead, 28% target margin) on its 2,150 sq ft mill-and-overlay preset:

FabricTotal costPrice
Without fabric$6,274.40$8,714.45
With fabric$7,646.10$10,619.59
Difference$1,371.70$1,905.14

The $1,182.50 of fabric material raises total cost by $1,371.70, not $1,182.50 — 16% overhead applies to the added material the same as it applies to everything else in the job ($1,182.50 × 1.16 = $1,371.70). Then, because price is total cost divided by (1 − 28%), that $1,371.70 of added cost turns into $1,905.14 of added price. Charging only the $1,182.50 material line — writing "+fabric, $1,182.50" on the bid instead of re-running the job through the calculator — leaves $722.64 of overhead and margin uncollected on this one job.

Overhead and margin apply to every dollar of scope, not just labor

It is easy to treat overhead and margin as something that lives on the labor and the base mix tons, and to pass a late add-on through at its raw material cost because it feels like "just materials." This calculator does not draw that line: overhead is a percentage of total direct cost, and price is total cost marked up to the target margin, whichever line the cost sits on. A material cost added after the estimate is drafted — fabric, a permit fee, extra gravel — carries the same overhead and margin share as everything already in the bid, or the bid quietly stops hitting its own target margin on the jobs that use it.

How to use the comparison

Open the asphalt driveway paving bid calculator, load the "2,000 sq ft mill-and-overlay, 2.5 in, fabric over cracks" preset, and toggle the fabric checkbox on and off to see the price move by $1,905.14 rather than by the $1,182.50 material line alone. This is the same arithmetic as how much to charge to pave a driveway and this calculator vs. a flat rate per square foot.

Common questions

Should I only charge material cost for paving fabric?

No. At this calculator's own default crew rates (16% overhead, 28% target margin), adding paving fabric to a 2,150 square foot mill-and-overlay costs $1,182.50 in material (2,150 sq ft x $0.55/sq ft) but should add $1,905.14 to the price. Charging only the $1,182.50 material line leaves $722.64 of overhead and margin uncollected on that job.

Where does the extra $722.64 come from?

Overhead first, then margin, in that order. The $1,182.50 of fabric material raises total cost by $1,371.70 once 16% overhead is applied on top of it ($1,182.50 + $189.20 overhead). Because price is total cost divided by (1 minus the 28% target margin), that $1,371.70 of added cost turns into $1,905.14 of added price — not the $1,182.50 the material alone cost.

Does fabric change the price on every job?

No. Fabric is its own checkbox, off by default, and adds nothing when left unchecked. It only changes the price on the square footage it actually covers — this calculator's own fabric-over-cracks preset covers a 2,000 square foot driveway plus a 150 square foot apron, 2,150 square feet in total.

Is this specific to fabric, or true of any add-on?

Any material line added after the estimate is drafted has the same gap: overhead and margin are set as a share of total cost and total price, not of the base scope alone, so a cost added without re-running the calculation is added at its raw material price — short by whatever overhead and margin that line was supposed to carry.

vs-a-flat-rate-per-square-foot.html.text:
← Asphalt Driveway Paving Bid Calculator

This calculator vs. a flat rate per square foot

"$3.50 a square foot" is not a price for a driveway — it is a price for one specific method, thickness, and scope, quietly applied to every driveway that walks in the door.

What a flat per-foot rate is

A flat rate is the fastest way to quote: multiply the paved square footage by a number and read off a price. Homeowners shop it because it is easy to compare between bids, and crews use it because it needs no takeoff. It is also the rate a customer holding a postcard or a competitor's website will ask you to match.

The number behind it was set for one job — one method, one thickness, no apron, no failed base, minimal sawcut — and then reused for every driveway afterward, whether or not the next driveway looks anything like the one the rate was built on.

What this calculator is

This page keeps no account and sends nothing to a server. You enter the driveway's square footage, thickness, and paving method (overlay, mill-and-overlay, or full-depth), the street apron, a failed-base patch, the sawcut, and your loaded labor and overhead. It converts area and thickness into mix tons by method, adds milling, demo, base-gravel, and sawcut hours separately, and returns a walk-away price below which the job loses money — for this driveway, not a generic one.

What a flat per-foot rate doesWhat this calculator does instead
Charges the same $/sq ft whether the job is an 800 sq ft 2-inch overlay or a 1,000 sq ft 3-inch full-depth replacement — a several-times difference in mix tons for a similar floor area. Converts each method's area and thickness into compacted mix tons from the asphalt's own density, so the tonnage tracks the job actually described, not the floor plan alone.
Prices "the driveway" as one paved area, with no separate line for the street apron, a failed-base patch, or the sawcut at the garage. Times the apron at its own thickness, failed base at gravel tons and demo hours, and sawcut at hours per lineal foot, so that scope shows up instead of being absorbed into the paved area or skipped.
Assumes sound existing asphalt underneath, so a job needing a failed-base patch gets quoted the same as one that does not. Adds demo, dump, and gravel-base cost only when that scope is turned on, so the two jobs price differently — about $4,700 walk-away versus a $3,780 flat quote on the same 1,080 sq ft of paved area once a 200 sq ft failed base and an 80 sq ft apron are real.
Bakes payroll burden into a round "labor rate" nobody re-derives, so the rate quietly drifts from the crew's real loaded cost. Loads the entered hourly wage by the entered payroll-burden percentage every time, so the labor cost tracks the actual burden rather than a memorized rate.
Gives the crew a price to quote, not a number to check a quote against. Reports the walk-away price, the effective hourly rate, and a three-method comparison on the same driveway, so a shopped price can be scored against real cost before the crew commits to it.

A flat rate is not wrong because it is simple — it is wrong when it is applied outside the one job it was built for, and nothing about a postcard rate tells you when that has happened. This calculator does not replace judgment about your market; it replaces the arithmetic a flat rate skips.

Common questions

Why does a flat rate per square foot get asphalt paving wrong?

Because mix tons come from thickness and method, not from the floor area alone. An 800 square foot overlay at 2 inches needs a fraction of the hot-mix a 1,000 square foot full-depth job at 3 inches needs, before the apron or a failed base is even counted. A flat rate charges both the same and is wrong on one of them every time.

What does a flat rate usually leave out entirely?

The street apron, a failed base, and the sawcut. A 4-inch apron at the street is its own thicker lift, a failed base means demo, dump, and gravel before a single ton of mix goes down, and a clean sawcut edge is its own hour stack. A rate built around "square feet of driveway" has nowhere to put any of that.

What happens when the base has failed?

A flat overlay rate assumes sound existing asphalt underneath. On a real 1,000 square foot job with a 200 square foot failed-base patch and an 80 square foot apron, the walk-away cost this calculator returns is about $4,700 — while a $3.50-a-square-foot quote on that same paved area comes to about $3,780. Quoting the flat rate on that driveway loses money before the crew leaves the yard.

Is a flat rate ever the right way to quote?

For a narrow band of near-identical jobs — same method, same thickness, no apron, no failed base, minimal sawcut — a flat rate can land close. The risk is applying it outside that band without noticing, because the postcard rate does not know which band a given driveway is in and neither does the crew until they measure it.

Does this calculator know what to charge in my market?

No. It has no data on local rates, mix prices, or what competitors charge. It takes the wage, mix cost, and overhead you enter and turns them into a walk-away price for the method, area, and scope you describe — the arithmetic a flat rate skips, not a market survey.

Nothing here says or implies that quoting a flat rate per square foot is a bad-faith practice — it is a common, honest shortcut that works until the job stops matching the one the rate was set on. This page describes where that shortcut breaks down, not a fault in anyone who uses it. The $3,780 and $4,700 figures above are this calculator's own arithmetic on the example job described in its README, not a claim about any specific contractor's real costs.

Open the Asphalt Driveway Paving Bid Calculator and price your own job.

This calculator vs. JobNimbus

Two different shapes: JobNimbus is an account-based CRM and job management platform for running an exterior contractor's whole lead-to-job pipeline. This page is a free, private worksheet for one question — what should this driveway cost, given its method, thickness, apron, and failed base, before you quote it.

What each tool is for

JobNimbus, founded in 2013 by Ben Hodson, Nick Wood, and Jason Wood and headquartered in Lehi, Utah, is a CRM and job management platform built for roofing, siding, gutter, and other exterior contractors. It covers lead capture and tracking, estimating, scheduling, invoicing, and job management for a whole company across every crew and every job, sold as an ongoing subscription account. JobNimbus's own pricing page is not reachable from this session to confirm today's exact plan names or dollar figures, so no price for it is invented here: only its well-documented identity, founders, headquarters, and category are stated, and no dollar amount for JobNimbus appears on this page.

This calculator does none of what JobNimbus does. It does not track a lead, schedule a crew, or invoice a customer across jobs. It takes one asphalt-driveway job — square footage, paving method (overlay, mill-and-overlay, or full-depth reclaim), asphalt thickness, street apron square footage, failed-base area needing full excavation and new stone, geotextile fabric, sawcutting, tack coat, demo and dump, plus loaded crew wage, payroll burden, travel, overhead, and target margin — and turns that into the price, the mix tons ordered, the price per square foot, and the walk-away price below which the job loses money, plus a printable customer proposal with a deposit split and a price-held date. It runs free in any browser, keeps no account, and uploads nothing you type.

Should I use this calculator or JobNimbus?

They do different jobs, and a paving company of any size will likely end up touching both eventually. JobNimbus, founded in 2013 by Ben Hodson, Nick Wood, and Jason Wood and headquartered in Lehi, Utah, is a CRM and job management platform built for roofing, siding, gutter, and other exterior contractors, covering lead tracking, estimates, scheduling, and invoicing across a whole business, sold as an ongoing subscription account. It runs free in any browser, keeps no account, and uploads nothing you type.
